evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The counterion is essential for opsin-based pigments to absorb visible light.
source: This counterion is essential for opsin-based pigments to absorb visible light, and the residues serving as the counterion are highly conserved across opsins (Nathans, 1990; Terakita, 2005; Terakita et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The residues serving as the counterion are highly conserved across opsins.
source: This counterion is essential for opsin-based pigments to absorb visible light, and the residues serving as the counterion are highly conserved across opsins (Nathans, 1990; Terakita, 2005; Terakita et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Three experimentally confirmed sites for the counterion have been identified in animal opsins: 94 in helix 2, 113 in helix 3, and 181 in extracellular loop 2.
source: To date, three experimentally confirmed sites for the counterion have been identified in animal opsins: 94 in helix 2 (Gerrard et al., 2018), 113 in helix 3 (Nathans, 1990; Sakai et al., 2022; Sakmar et al., 1989; Zhukovsky and Oprian, 1989), and 181 in extracellular loop 2 (Nagata et al., 2019; Terakita et al., 2004; Terakita et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Some opsins belonging to the ASO-II group lack glutamic or aspartic acid at any of the established counterion positions.
source: Remarkably, some opsins belonging to the ASO-II group lack glutamic or aspartic acid at any of these established counterion positions (Gornik et al., 2021; Mason et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Cl− and Glu292, respectively, act as counterions for the protonated Schiff base of the dark state and photoproduct of Antho2a.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Cl− and Glu292, respectively, act as counterions for the protonated Schiff base of the dark state and photoproduct of Antho2a.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on inference from spectroscopic and computational data.

claim: Antho2a exhibits counterion switching from exogenous anion to a specific amino acid residue upon light irradiation.
source: This represents a unique example of counterion switching from exogenous anion to a specific amino acid residue upon light irradiation (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on inference from the spectroscopic data. Figure 7 provides a visual representation.

claim: Opsins in the ASO-II group may share a spectral tuning mechanism based on the Cl− counterion.
source: Our spectroscopic data also showed that the other visual light-sensitive opsin, Antho2c, exhibited the Cl− dependency on the Schiff base pKa of the dark state, which suggested that opsins in the ASO-II group may share a spectral tuning mechanism based on the Cl− counterion.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on inference from spectroscopic data of Antho2c.

claim: The positive charge of Arg113 in Antho2e disturbs interaction between the Cl− and the protonated Schiff base or completely inhibits Cl− binding, rendering Antho2e UV-sensitive.
source: We hypothesize that the positive charge of Arg113 disturbs interaction between the Cl− and the protonated Schiff base or that it completely inhibits Cl− binding, rendering Antho2e UV-sensitive.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is speculative.

claim: The λmax of a retinylidene Schiff base in solution increases with the ionic radius of halides acting as hydrogen bond acceptors (i.e. I−>Br−>Cl−).
source: Similarly, our results align with earlier observations that the λmax of a retinylidene Schiff base in solution increases with the ionic radius of halides acting as hydrogen bond acceptors (i.e. I−>Br−>Cl−) (Blatz et al., 1972).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The λmax of halorhodopsin from Natronobacterium pharaonic does not clearly correlate with halide ionic radius.
source: In contrast, the λmax of halorhodopsin from Natronobacterium pharaonic does not clearly correlate with halide ionic radius (Scharf and Engelhard, 1994), as the halide ion in this case is not a hydrogen-bonding acceptor of the protonated Schiff base (Kouyama et al., 2010; Mizuno et al., 2018).
